source: Yuan et al. (2025) NL2GenSym: Natural Language to Generative Symbolic Rules for SOAR via LLMs
finding: An LLM generator plus an LLM critic that runs each candidate rule set in real Soar turns natural-language Water Jug descriptions into working Soar rules. The task is writing Soar operator proposal, preference and impasse-handling rules.
numbers: 100 cases (25 easy, 25 medium, 30 hard, 20 variant with n=3). Gemini-2.5-Flash with framework: 86% success rate, average decision cycles 1.76x optimal. Qwen-max with framework: 91% SR, 1.98x optimal. Runs over 500,000 decision cycles count as failure.
limits: Single toy domain (Water Jug). Preprint. Success means the rules solve the puzzle in Soar, not that they are general.
agent_relevance: The program ran the candidate and fed back the real Soar trace. This matches our G2 (revise only from real output) and G3.

source: Yuan et al. (2025) NL2GenSym: Natural Language to Generative Symbolic Rules for SOAR via LLMs
finding: Baselines on the same 100 Water Jug cases show how weak plain prompting is for Soar rule writing.
numbers: Zero-shot: 0% for both Gemini-2.5-Pro and Qwen-max. One-shot: Gemini-Pro 55% SR, avg 20,344 decision cycles; Qwen 66% SR, 20,670 cycles. Hand-coded Soar baseline: 84% SR, avg 27,019 cycles (3,390x optimal); only 46.67% on hard cases.
limits: The manual baseline is one author-written rule set, not an expert benchmark.
agent_relevance: Even working rules can be thousands of times too slow. A pass check alone is not enough; step count must also be measured.

source: Yuan et al. (2025) NL2GenSym: Natural Language to Generative Symbolic Rules for SOAR via LLMs
finding: Ablation: the execution-grounded critic matters most.
numbers: Removing the critic: success down 23% overall, down 37% on hard and variant cases, and avg cycles above 1,000x minimum. Removing the basic Soar knowledge base: down 17%. Removing the case knowledge base: down 14%.
limits: Authors' ablations on the same toy dataset; no seeds or confidence intervals seen in the text I read.
agent_relevance: Supports a verifier that runs the artifact and returns its real trace as the key part, more than extra retrieved knowledge.

source: Yuan et al. (2025) NL2GenSym: Natural Language to Generative Symbolic Rules for SOAR via LLMs
finding: A smaller model plus the scaffold beat a larger model with plain prompting.
numbers: Gemini-2.5-Flash with NL2GenSym 86% SR vs Gemini-2.5-Pro one-shot 55% SR (Pro about 2,500x optimal cycles vs 1.76x). Hard-case gain for Gemini: +56.67 points over one-shot.
limits: Authors call it preliminary. One domain. Token cost of the loop is not reported.
agent_relevance: A scaffold can beat model scale on a checkable task. For G7 we would need the token cost, which this paper does not give.

source: Yuan et al. (2025) NL2GenSym: Natural Language to Generative Symbolic Rules for SOAR via LLMs
finding: The critic's feedback on one run flagged that the generated agent fell into a state no-change impasse and looped forever, and asked for detection and halting for all five impasse names.
numbers: Critic list: state no-change, operator no-change, tie, conflict, constraint-failure. In the example a syntax error in a preference rule left too few rules loaded, and the loop followed.
quote: ensure reliable detection and halting for all impasse types
limits: One example trace in the appendix, not a measured rate of impasse types.
agent_relevance: Loops from no-change are a common failure and need a counter-based detector. Our no-change trigger (no pass in two rounds) is the same idea.

source: CogRec authors (2025) CogRec: A Cognitive Recommender Agent Fusing LLMs and Soar
finding: Soar runs the decision cycle. When an impasse arises (the case study is a tie between several sci-fi films), Soar sends a structured query to DeepSeek-V3. The answer is turned into a new rule by chunking.
numbers: About 500 initial rules from LLM bootstrapping, about 10 prompt templates per dataset. Datasets ML-1M, Movies, Yelp. Metrics HR@10/20 and NDCG@10/20.
limits: Framework paper. No seeds, variance or significance tests seen. Reported training details (embedding size 128, Adam) sit oddly with a symbolic agent, so the exact pipeline is unclear.
agent_relevance: The only LLM agent I found where the impasse itself is the call-the-LLM trigger and the result is stored as a reusable rule.

source: CogRec authors (2025) CogRec: A Cognitive Recommender Agent Fusing LLMs and Soar
finding: CogRec beat all baselines, but the gain over a plain LLM is small.
numbers: ML-1M HR@10: CogRec 0.3124, LLM-Direct (DeepSeek-V3) 0.2901, GPT4Rec 0.2956, SASRec 0.2815, pure Soar with about 20 hand rules 0.0511. Yelp HR@10: CogRec 0.2247 vs LLM-Direct 0.2053. Paper reports +4.4% to +9.1% over the best baseline.
limits: Gain over LLM-Direct is about +7.7% relative on ML-1M HR@10. The best baseline differs per column. Token or call cost not compared.
agent_relevance: An impasse-driven hybrid gives a modest gain. It is not evidence of large gains on reasoning tasks.

source: CogRec authors (2025) CogRec: A Cognitive Recommender Agent Fusing LLMs and Soar
finding: Ablations: without chunking performance falls close to the plain LLM; without LLM bootstrapping it falls sharply. LLM-call frequency drops over time only with chunking.
numbers: Results are in figures only. Text: without chunking 'approaching that of LLM-Direct'; call frequency 'converging to a low, stable plateau' with chunking and 'consistently high' without.
limits: No exact numbers in the text; figure values not extracted. Apparently one run per setting.
agent_relevance: The stored shortcut is what pays. A stored, conditioned result from a subgoal should cut later calls.

source: CogRec authors (2025) CogRec: A Cognitive Recommender Agent Fusing LLMs and Soar
finding: Long-tail items: all models lose accuracy; CogRec loses less than SASRec and LLM-Direct.
numbers: Head = top 20% of items, long tail = bottom 80% by frequency; N@10 on ML-1M, shown in a figure only.
limits: No numbers in text.
agent_relevance: Minor for us.

source: Fan and Lan (2026) From Cognitive Architectures to Language Agents: A Mechanism-Level Review
finding: The review maps Soar's chain (typed impasse, protected substate, typed result return, chunking of only the conditions that mattered) onto LLM agent work. The pieces exist separately but no reviewed system couples all of them.
numbers: Evidence code for Soar-to-typed-recovery: E3/D3. Reflexion and AgentHER failure learning: E3/D4. Missing pieces listed: parent isolation, substate decision cycle, typed result return, safe compilation.
quote: No reviewed system couples typed impasse, protected branch, typed return, and condition-safe compilation.
limits: The grades are the review's own judgment. It relies on cited preprints and has no new experiments.
agent_relevance: Their gap is our opportunity: typed trigger, sandboxed attempt, typed return, stored rule with preconditions.

source: Fan and Lan (2026) From Cognitive Architectures to Language Agents: A Mechanism-Level Review
finding: The review argues that in Soar the impasse is a control state with force before any recovery content exists, while in LLM agents failure is just content in the prompt.
numbers: Cites PALADIN, AgentDebugX, Shepherd, AgentHER, Reflexion as modern pieces; ownership is split across classifier, recovery generator, memory process and host loop.
limits: Argument, not measurement. The authors warn a generated recovery can change state before its diagnosis is validated.
agent_relevance: Supports the program owning the transition (SCHEMA section 1).

source: Fan and Lan (2026) From Cognitive Architectures to Language Agents: A Mechanism-Level Review
finding: The review treats uncertainty-triggered help (KnowNo) and runtime scheduling (AIOS) as the closest analog of EPIC/Sigma resource control, and says shared uncertainty for budget, interrupts and stopping is still open.
numbers: Residual couplings: ACT-R utility-latency law; Soar typed impasse plus chunking; EPIC/Sigma uncertainty budget. One closed candidate: GraSP (verify, repair, replan, fall back to ReAct).
limits: No numbers extracted.
agent_relevance: Links to the Adaptive stopping and metareasoning subfield (not covered here).

source: Laird (2022) Introduction to the Soar Cognitive Architecture
finding: Decision cycle: rules propose operators, rules create preferences (better, equal, best, worst, reject, numeric), and a fixed procedure picks one. If preferences are inconclusive or in conflict, no operator is picked and an impasse arises.
numbers: About 50 ms per decision cycle is needed for real-time behavior. TacAir-Soar is over 8000 rules.
limits: Vendor overview; no replication.
agent_relevance: Our S6 picks among candidates by code, not by model, like the fixed decision procedure.

source: Laird (2022) Introduction to the Soar Cognitive Architecture
finding: Impasse types. The main text lists three groups by the failed knowledge (state no-change, operator tie/conflict, operator no-change). The glossary says there are technically four: state no-change, operator no-change (same operator for two or more decisions), tie, conflict. Constraint-failure is not in this paper.
numbers: Substate: new state linked to its superstate, own preference memory, access to superstate; one substate per state; substates nest into a stack. An impasse is resolved when a new decision can be made or another impasse arises; the substate data is then removed.
quote: Soar embraces a philosophy that additional relevant knowledge can be obtained through additional deliberate reasoning
limits: Constraint-failure (from require/prohibit conflicts) appears in NL2GenSym's list but I did not open the Soar manual this session.
agent_relevance: Typed triggers have different handlers: no-change means make new operators; tie means evaluate and add preferences; operator no-change means decompose or wait.

source: Laird (2022) Introduction to the Soar Cognitive Architecture
finding: What chunking learns depends on the impasse type. State no-change gives operator proposal rules; tie or conflict gives evaluation rules (search control, value functions); operator no-change gives operator application rules; any impasse can give elaboration rules.
numbers: Soar uses one mechanism for deliberation and meta-reasoning, in contrast to MIDCA and CLARION which use separate meta modules.
limits: Learned rules are only as general as the substate reasoning.
agent_relevance: Each trigger type could have its own stored-rule type in our subgoal library (links to the Soar chunking subfield).

source: Sumers, Yao, Narasimhan, Griffiths (2024) Cognitive Architectures for Language Agents (CoALA)
finding: CoALA maps LLM agents onto Soar-like parts: memories, action space, and a decision cycle with propose, evaluate, select. Its selection step either picks an action or rejects all and loops back to proposal.
numbers: Evaluation can use heuristics, LLM perplexity, learned values or LLM reasoning; selection by argmax, softmax or majority vote.
quote: If no actions are valid, or multiple actions tie, then an impasse occurs.
limits: Conceptual framework; no new experiments. CoALA has no typed impasse and no substate with a return type; it has only the loop back.
agent_relevance: The standard bridge between Soar and LLM agents. The missing piece is exactly the typed impasse.

source: Sumers, Yao, Narasimhan, Griffiths (2024) Cognitive Architectures for Language Agents (CoALA)
finding: CoALA classifies Tree of Thoughts as an agent with only reasoning actions and an explicit propose-evaluate-select search; ReAct has a fixed decision cycle with no memory.
numbers: ToT is described as a special agent with one external action: submitting a final solution.
limits: Classification by the authors.
agent_relevance: Tie resolution by lookahead (ToT) is the LLM version of Soar's tie substate, but ToT runs it always, not only on a tie.

source: Yao et al. (2023) Tree of Thoughts: Deliberate Problem Solving with LLMs
finding: Propose-then-evaluate search over partial thoughts is the closest published LLM analog of Soar's tie-substate lookahead.
numbers: Game of 24 with GPT-4: ToT b=5 74%, b=1 45%, CoT 4.0%, IO 7.3%, CoT-SC k=100 9.0%, CoT best of 100 49%, IO best of 100 33%.
limits: Task chosen because it needs search; authors say ToT may not be needed where GPT-4 already does well.
agent_relevance: Search pays on search-shaped tasks; evaluating candidates beats sampling more.

source: Yao et al. (2023) Tree of Thoughts: Deliberate Problem Solving with LLMs
finding: Cost and component analysis for ToT.
numbers: ToT used about 5.5k completion tokens per Game-of-24 case, near 100 CoT trials (6.7k), at $0.74 vs $0.47 for best-of-100 CoT (49%). GPT-3.5 with ToT 19%. GPT-4 generation with GPT-3.5 evaluation 64%; GPT-3.5 generation with GPT-4 evaluation 31%.
limits: Run May 2023 on one model family.
agent_relevance: At similar tokens ToT beat best-of-100 (74% vs 49%). Generation was the bottleneck, not evaluation, on this task.

source: Shinn et al. (2023) Reflexion: Language Agents with Verbal Reinforcement Learning
finding: Reflexion fires self-reflection from an impasse-like counter. In ALFWorld a hand-written heuristic triggers reflection when the same action gets the same response for more than 3 cycles, or after 30 actions.
numbers: ReAct+Reflexion solved 130 of 134 ALFWorld tasks; ReAct alone stalled between trials 6 and 7. Paper reports +22% ALFWorld, +20% HotPotQA, +11% HumanEval over baselines; 91% HumanEval pass@1 vs GPT-4 80%.
quote: if the agent executes the same action and receives the same response for more than 3 cycles
limits: The trigger is a simple repeat/length counter, not a typed impasse. Gains rely on an environment signal.
agent_relevance: Soar's operator no-change (same operator for two decisions) is mechanically this repeat counter. Code-run counters work.

source: Kirk, Wray, Lindes, Laird (2024) Improving Knowledge Extraction from LLMs for Task Learning through Agent Analysis (STARS)
finding: A Soar-based embodied agent gets goal descriptions from an LLM. STARS: beam-search tree of responses, then the agent analyzes and repairs each against what it can ground, then selects one. Learned task knowledge stays in Soar, so the LLM is not needed on the second try.
numbers: Completion without human help on three tasks: baseline 52.5% (tidy kitchen), 66.7% (store groceries), 35.7% (organize office); STARS 77.5%, 94.4%, 92.9%. With oversight both reach 100%. On a repeat of the task: 100% with no LLM call.
limits: Simulation, three tasks, GPT-3 for generation and GPT-4 for selection, one run per condition (10 runs of STARS showed little variation).
agent_relevance: Checking candidates against the agent's own grounded state before use lifts results, and learned results can be reused without the model.

source: Kirk, Wray, Lindes, Laird (2024) Improving Knowledge Extraction from LLMs for Task Learning through Agent Analysis (STARS)
finding: Most raw LLM answers are unusable for the agent. The search tree alone gave no gain; the analysis and repair step produced the gain.
numbers: Share of LLM responses not viable: over 70% (kitchen), 58% (groceries), 85% (office). Situationally relevant: 13%, 14%, 5%. Oversight words cut from 403 to 127 (kitchen), 92 to 44, 184 to 60.
limits: The viability checks are hand-built for this agent's body and world.
agent_relevance: Generating more options without a check does nothing; the check is the value. Matches G3 and G5.

source: Kirk, Wray, Lindes, Laird (2024) Improving Knowledge Extraction from LLMs for Task Learning through Agent Analysis (STARS)
finding: The LLM selection step needed context the agent had not given. With a system prompt of three facts, kitchen completion rose from 77.5% to 92.5%.
numbers: Facts given: dishware on the table is dirty, bottles are empty, non-perishable food goes in the pantry.
limits: The context was supplied by the authors after they saw the failure.
agent_relevance: Selection by a model is fragile without world facts; a tie needs real evaluation knowledge.

source: Zhu and Simmons (2024) Bootstrapping Cognitive Agents with a Large Language Model
finding: The agent keeps a task stack inspired by the Soar impasse mechanism and the ACT-R goal module. If no stored production applies (a no-change style gap), it summarizes state and asks an LLM for an action and a production rule to reuse.
numbers: Household tasks, 15 instances per family. Find: action-only 14/15, bootstrapped 15/15 with 12/15 solved with no LLM call; query tokens 54,754 vs 917. Slice and clear: 15/15 both; bootstrapped used 0 tokens vs 102,807 and 18,925.
limits: Simulated kitchen. Steps equal for find and slice (p=0.446, 0.347) but bootstrapped took longer in clearing (p=0.001) because a reused rule forced each object into its own empty cabinet. About 1,400 bootstrapping steps; learned rules differ between runs.
agent_relevance: Reused rules cut tokens by over 98%, but a stored rule can quietly change behavior; test stored rules on a second problem.

source: Vuddanti et al. (2025) PALADIN: Self-Correcting Language Model Agents to Cure Tool-Failure Cases
finding: PALADIN is a typed-recovery system: it detects a tool error, retrieves the nearest of 55+ exemplar failures from a seven-class taxonomy, and runs the matched recovery action (retry, reformat, switch tool, terminate). Trained with LoRA on 50,000+ failure-injected trajectories.
numbers: Recovery rate: vanilla 23.75%, ToolBench 32.76%, CRITIC 76.34%, PALADIN 89.68% (Gemma-3 12B on PaladinEval). Claims 95.2% of recovery kept on unseen tool APIs. Other model and eval cells show +5 to +14 points over the best baseline.
limits: Simulated tool failures; GPT-5 used as simulator and grader; needs fine-tuning; efficiency score lower than rivals.
agent_relevance: The failure type chooses the response, as impasse types do in Soar. It needs training, so it is not directly our approach.

source: Recovery Is a Decision - But Whose? Live Agents Overturn Replay Evaluations of Tool-Failure Triage (NeurIPS 2026)
finding: Seen only in a search result: on 16,163 real failure events from PALADIN's corpus, a simple logistic-regression controller matched annotated recovery decisions more often than PALADIN's retrieval or rule orchestration.
numbers: About 63.6% vs about 43% agreement (search snippet only).
limits: Not opened. Treat as unverified.
agent_relevance: If true, learned retrieval of failure type adds little over a plain classifier; keep trigger logic simple and in code.

source: Zhu et al. (2026) AgentDebugX: Failure Observability, Attribution and Recovery in LLM Agents
finding: A closed loop Detect, Attribute, Recover, Rerun for LLM agents. Hard cases go to a multi-round diagnosis agent (DeepDebug).
numbers: Who&When attribution (strict agent-and-step): 28.8% with qwen3.5-9b vs 21.7% for the best single-pass baseline. GAIA validation (165 tasks): vanilla 55.8%; 73 failures re-run once; Level-2 accuracy 48.8 to 61.6; more than double the repairs of decoupled Reflexion, CRITIC and AutoManual.
limits: Authors say the test measures the full recipe, not attribution alone. One re-run per failure. Small 9B model.
agent_relevance: A diagnosis that names the step and cites evidence beat a generic failure summary as input to the retry. Matches G2.

source: Yu et al. (2026) Shepherd: Programmable Meta-Agents via Reversible Agentic Execution Traces
finding: Shepherd gives agent runs a git-like reversible trace: fork, revert and replay from any past state. This is the nearest engineering analog of a protected substate that does not disturb the parent.
numbers: Fork takes 134-143 ms, 2-3% of one agent turn; prompt-cache hit about 95%. A runtime supervisor lifts CooperBench pair pass rate 28.8% to 54.7% (Opus meta-agent; solo ceiling 57.2%). The counterfactual optimizer beats MetaHarness on Terminal-Bench 2.0 by 12.8% with 58% lower wall-clock.
limits: No typed impasse and no learned rule; the meta-agent decides when to intervene by its own judgment.
agent_relevance: Cheap fork-and-return of a trial attempt is practical; our substate can be a forked attempt whose only output is a result.

source: Agentic Cognitive Depth: Operational Criteria for Evaluating LLM Agents (2026)
finding: Names run-level metacognitive monitoring as the missing layer in LLM agents and cites Soar impasse-driven subgoaling as the architecture that supplied meta-level control.
numbers: Says retry loops such as Reflexion 'usually revise a local answer and leave the full run unregulated'.
quote: Soar's impasse-driven subgoaling provided meta-level control in a cognitive architecture
limits: Position paper with criteria; no measured effect from impasse control.
agent_relevance: Supports a trigger layer above the attempt loop.

source: Illusion of Thinking (2025), reasoning models on controllable puzzles
finding: Only the abstract page was fetched, not the paper. Reasoning models show accuracy collapse past a puzzle complexity, reduce reasoning effort near collapse, and fail to use a given explicit algorithm reliably.
numbers: No thresholds read. Three regimes: plain LLM better at low complexity, reasoning model better at medium, both collapse at high.
limits: Abstract only. Rebuttals exist that I did not open.
agent_relevance: Deep goal-stack puzzles may break the model; a program should hold the goal stack.

source: Romero et al. (2023) Synergistic Integration of LLMs and Cognitive Architectures for Robust AI
finding: Exploratory CMU paper proposing ways to combine LLMs with cognitive architectures such as Soar and ACT-R; argues architectures bring bounded rationality and LLMs bring knowledge. Includes an example where ChatGPT generates ACT-R production rules.
numbers: Preliminary data only; no benchmark numbers.
limits: Proposal paper. Does not test impasses.
agent_relevance: Context only; supports the hybrid direction without numbers.
